title: Tax ownership: one sales order calculates the wrong tax
prompt: A sales order calculates a tax amount that the business says is wrong. Sales proposes changing the tax condition manually. Diagnose the first wrong decision and assign ownership before correcting the document.
expected_points: Start with the legal and business tax rule that should apply; Tax or Finance owns the policy, not the sales-order user.
Check departure, destination, ship-to, plant, company, registration, and jurisdiction context before changing the final tax amount.
Validate customer and material tax classifications and other reusable taxability inputs in master data.
Trace pricing procedure, tax condition, access, condition record, tax code, and calculation path.
If an external tax engine is authoritative, prove request inputs, response, mapping, version, and fallback separately from SAP pricing.
Close with consistent sales order, billing, tax posting, and FI evidence rather than a manual tax override.
follow_up_questions: What changes if only one country uses an external tax engine?
Who owns the correction if the customer tax classification is wrong but pricing configuration is correct?
red_flags: Calls every tax issue an SD configuration problem
Changes a customer exception in code without a legal-policy owner

title: EWM execution: warehouse complete, ERP state incomplete
prompt: The warehouse says picking and loading are complete in EWM, but the S/4HANA delivery and inventory state do not show the expected goods issue. Operations proposes a manual ERP goods movement. Diagnose the ownership and recovery path.
expected_points: Start with the S/4 business delivery or goods-movement request and the quantity expected to move.
Trace the distributed EWM warehouse request, warehouse tasks, warehouse orders, stock, handling-unit, batch, or serial context as relevant.
Prove physical execution from task confirmation and exceptions rather than from planned warehouse tasks.
Check the EWM-to-S/4 delivery confirmation or integration state and identify the first missing handoff.
Do not post a manual ERP goods movement before reconciling physical warehouse state because it can create a second inconsistency.
Close only when EWM execution, S/4 delivery status, material document, inventory, and downstream billing or planning effects agree.
follow_up_questions: What if EWM task confirmation is missing even though operators say the goods moved?
What changes when a non-SAP automation system controls the physical conveyor execution?
red_flags: Posts PGI manually in S/4 to make status green
Assumes completed picking proves ERP goods issue
Looks only at the integration monitor without warehouse-task evidence

title: aATP priority: strategic customer asks for scarce supply
prompt: Supply is short. A strategic customer asks Sales to increase its confirmation even though quantities are already confirmed to other customers and regions. Decide how the priority should be represented and who owns the customer impact.
expected_points: Separate the business scarce-supply policy from the technical ATP confirmation of one order.
Use Product Allocation when the business wants upper consumption limits for defined groups.
Use Supply Protection when minimum quantities must remain protected for defined demand groups.
Use Backorder Processing with explicit segments and confirmation strategies when existing confirmations must be reprioritized after supply or demand changes.
Explain that improving one confirmation can reduce, delay, or remove another confirmation, so the policy and customer impact need an accountable business owner.
Keep Sales responsible for customer communication while avoiding ad hoc manual confirmation changes that bypass the reusable supply policy.
follow_up_questions: How can Product Allocation and Supply Protection block each other if their characteristics are poorly aligned?
What evidence would you review before running BOP on a high-demand material?
red_flags: Manually increases the VIP order without naming who loses supply
Treats BOP as a technical batch job with no customer impact
Says ATP itself owns commercial priority

title: Message ordering: update overtakes create
prompt: An external system sends create and update events for the same sales object. Parallel processing allows the update to reach SAP before the create. The team proposes putting every message for every customer into one exclusive queue. Design the ordering boundary.
expected_points: State the business invariant first: for the same business object, create must complete before dependent update or cancel events.
Define the narrowest sequence key such as one order or business-object stream instead of serializing unrelated customers or documents.
Separate idempotency from ordering: duplicate-safe processing does not make out-of-order state transitions valid.
Use ordered processing such as EOIO or an exclusive/partitioned queue only for the required sequence scope and make the throughput cost explicit.
Define what happens when one predecessor fails because strict ordering can block all successors in that stream.
Prove end-to-end order across sender, middleware, protocol, receiver, and business-state reconciliation rather than relying on queue order alone.
follow_up_questions: When would version checks be better than strict queue ordering?
What happens to throughput and recovery if the whole interface uses one exclusive queue?
red_flags: Serializes the entire landscape without defining a business key
Ignores blocked successors when one predecessor fails
